# Verify the Load, Don't Declare It

A data pipeline ends with a **query whose result can be wrong**, not with a status row saying it went
fine. The distinction sounds pedantic until you have shipped an empty warehouse that logged
`'Success'` five times.

> "A row count is a fact; a status table populated with 'Success' literals is a claim. These queries
> are cheap and they fail loudly."
> — Data-Warehousing-and-Business-Intelligence/sql/02_star_schema/02_load_star_schema.sql, 2026-07-25

## Both sides of the argument are in one repository

The unusual thing about [[data-warehousing-and-business-intelligence]] is that it ships the
counter-example alongside the pattern. `etl/ssis/Package.dtsx` creates a `load_status` table and
inserts one `'Success'` literal per table, unconditionally — see [[ssis]]. The hand-written
`sql/02_star_schema/` version deletes that idea and replaces it with three things that can fail:

1. **A row-count roll-call** — a `UNION ALL` returning the count of all five tables in one result set.
   Zero rows anywhere is visible at a glance.
2. **Anti-join integrity checks** — `NOT EXISTS` against the parent dimension for orphaned order
   dates and for fact rows with no product, each returning a `Failures` count. The comment beside
   them reads "Referential integrity actually holds, rather than being asserted."
3. **Property checks on the derived column**, in the price mart:

> "A working RSI spends most of its life between 30 and 70. If nearly every row sits at an extreme,
> the window frame is not doing its job."
> — Data-Warehousing-and-Business-Intelligence/project/twtr/sql/03_technical_indicators.sql, 2026-07-25

That third one is the strongest form. A row count catches an empty load; a foreign-key check catches
a broken join; only a **property of the output distribution** catches a load that ran, joined
cleanly, and computed the wrong thing. The same script also asserts the exact warm-up count — thirteen
rows with no indicator, the days before the first full window — which is a check on
[[window-function-frames]] rather than on the data.

## Why the checks live *inside* the load script

The verification is section 6 of the load, not a separate file someone might not run. It is also the
reason the dimension is built from the source rather than from the fact table — the load script's own
header explains that the alternative would "build cleanly and contain nothing", which is precisely
the failure a `'Success'` row cannot see. See [[etl-load-order]] and [[fact-grain]].

## The same discipline, enforced rather than written

[[labour-fraud-analysis]] takes the pattern the rest of the way, because it has somewhere to enforce
it:

- `build_db.py` loads with `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`, so a successful build **is** the FK proof.
- `test_counts_match_manifest` reconciles every CSV's row count against a committed manifest — a real
  count-vs-expectation check, not a self-report.
- `make validate` "must print RESULT: PASS" — the privacy analogue, [[disclosure-gate]].
- All of it runs on every push via [[github-actions]].

## The honest limit

In the warehousing repo the pattern is **written but never executed and recorded**. Every check is a
query needing a live [[sql-server]] with both AdventureWorks databases attached; no output, log or
expected-count file is committed anywhere in the tree. "0 orphans" is a query, not a result. The
difference between the two repositories is not the idea — it is whether a machine other than the
author's ever runs it. See [[generated-audit-artifact]] and [[reproducible-analysis]].
